Beyond sensors: software, networks and security

MTDI Studio · October 2026

MTDI was born measuring magnetic and electric fields, but nothing in its pillars depends on physics. A channel is a stream of numbers with a unit, an expected rate and a noise floor. That describes a lot of technology.

Computers and single-board computers

Host Health watches the machine MTDI runs on. Its CPU, memory, load and network each learn a normal level. An NVTRA rule flags outbound traffic that rises while compute stays normal: a backup explains it, and so would data leaving that should not. Running it on a Raspberry Pi turns the Pi into its own diagnostic instrument.

Networks

Network Watch's probe measures TCP connect latency and failure rate to one target. Environmental Intelligence learns what this particular link normally does, so "slow" means slow for this link, not slower than a number someone guessed.

Cybersecurity

Auth Watch counts failed and accepted authentications per window from a Linux auth log. A fixed threshold ("alert after 10 failures") is wrong in both directions: too noisy on a busy bastion host, too lax on a quiet one. Environmental Intelligence learns each host's own rhythm, and an NVTRA rule describes the brute-force pattern: failures far above normal, without matching successes. The rule also names the innocent explanation, a misconfigured client retrying stale credentials, because MTDI never claims more than its evidence.

Honest limits

MTDI watches numbers. It does not parse packets, scan for vulnerabilities or replace an intrusion detection system. It is a diagnostic layer that tells you when something departs from its own normal, and how much to trust the measurement that says so.
